kid: A book made for one year, with calendars, sky times, weather notes and advice.
more: A yearly reference book of calendars, sunrise and sunset times, seasonal advice for farmers and other facts; old almanacs are clues about life back then.

kid: How much warmer or cooler something is than its usual average.
more: The difference between a measurement and the long-term average for that place and date; scientists use anomalies to track change over time.

kid: A space ruler: one AU is how far Earth is from the Sun.
more: The Sun-Earth distance, about 150 million km, used to measure the solar system; light crosses one AU in about 8 minutes 20 seconds.

kid: The middle-ish number you get by adding numbers up and sharing them out evenly.
more: Add all the values, then divide by how many there are; climate averages and anomaly baselines are built this way from long records.

kid: A place or thing a tool cannot see well, so missing dots do not mean nothing.
more: The limits of a measurement: what it misses or gets wrong, like satellites underestimating thin new sea ice or having no view near the pole.
src: NSIDC: Arctic Sea Ice News FAQ

kid: An invisible gas in the air that plants take in and that burning fuel gives off.
more: A gas measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958; its amount in the air rises and falls each year with plant growth, on top of a long rise.
src: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory: CO2 trends

kid: The usual weather of a place over many, many years.
more: The average weather conditions of a place over a long time, usually 30 years or more; one storm or hot week is weather, not climate.

kid: Giant threads of matter in space, with galaxies sitting along them like beads.
more: The universe's largest pattern: filaments and sheets of mostly dark matter linking galaxies and clusters, mapped by inference rather than seen directly.
src: NASA Hubble: Mapping the Cosmic Web

kid: A bowl-shaped hole made when a space rock smashes into the ground.
more: A pit blasted out by an impacting asteroid, meteoroid or comet; with no wind or liquid water, Moon craters last billions of years.

kid: When we see just a thin curved sliver of the Moon lit up.
more: A phase showing a thin sliver of the sunlit side: waxing crescent just after new Moon, waning crescent just before the next one.

kid: Facts and numbers people collect so they can learn something.
more: Recorded information, often measurements in numbers, gathered to answer questions; every figure on this site comes from a named source's data.

kid: When the ground suddenly shakes because rocks underground move.
more: Shaking of Earth's surface caused by a sudden slip of rock along a fault in the crust, most often near the edges of tectonic plates.
src: NASA Space Place: What Is an Earthquake?

kid: A crack in Earth's rocky outer layer where the rocks can slip.
more: A break in the crust where blocks of rock move past each other; stress builds until the rock slips, causing an earthquake. California's San Andreas is one.
src: NASA Space Place: What Is an Earthquake?

kid: A huge family of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
more: A vast system of stars, gas and dust bound by gravity, holding millions to billions of stars; Andromeda is our nearest big neighbour.
src: NASA Imagine the Universe: Milky Way Galaxy

kid: When more than half of the Moon looks lit, but it is not full yet.
more: A phase when more than half of the Moon's face is lit: waxing gibbous grows toward full Moon, waning gibbous shrinks after it.

kid: A huge river of ice that moves very slowly over land.
more: Ice built up from snow that survives year after year, packed down into dense ice that slowly flows downhill under its own weight.

kid: The invisible pull that keeps us on the ground and the Moon near Earth.
more: A force pulling objects with mass toward each other; it keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and causes ocean tides, and gives you your weight.
src: NASA Space Place: What Is Gravity?

kid: A very hot place deep under Earth's plates that can make volcanoes.
more: A small, long-lasting, extra-hot region below a plate; as the plate moves over it, a chain of volcanoes like the Hawaiian Islands forms.

kid: A giant blanket of ice covering a huge area of land.
more: Land ice covering more than 50,000 square km; only Greenland and Antarctica have one today, and their meltwater raises sea level.

kid: Melted rock that comes out of a volcano.
more: Molten rock that erupts onto the surface from a vent or crack; it is called magma while it is still underground.

kid: How far light travels in one whole day: billions of kilometres.
more: The distance light covers in 24 hours, about 25.9 billion km; NASA calculated Voyager 1 would reach it on 18 November 2026.
src: NASA: Voyager 1: What is a light-day?

kid: How far light travels in one year. It measures distance, not time.
more: The distance light travels in one year, about 9 trillion km; used for distances to stars and galaxies.
src: NASA Space Place: What is a light-year?

kid: A giant spark of electricity that flashes in a storm.
more: A sudden electrical discharge inside a storm cloud or between cloud and ground, heating the air to about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.

kid: Hot, melted rock deep inside the Earth.
more: Molten rock with dissolved gas and crystals that forms deep underground; when it reaches the surface it is called lava.

kid: A number that tells how big an earthquake is.
more: The size of an earthquake at its source, measured with seismographs; each whole step up means about 32 times more energy released.
src: USGS: The Severity of an Earthquake

kid: The dark patches on the Moon, called seas, but they hold no water.
more: Latin for 'seas': huge impact basins on the Moon that filled with lava between about 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago.

kid: When animals take a long trip each season and then come back.
more: A seasonal round trip between habitats, made to find food, better conditions or a place to raise young, as monarchs and whales do.

kid: Our home galaxy, a giant spiral of billions of stars.
more: Our barred spiral galaxy, about 100,000 light-years across, with the Sun about 25,000 light-years from its centre.
src: NASA Imagine the Universe: Milky Way Galaxy

kid: The shape of the lit part of the Moon that we see on a given night.
more: How much of the Moon's sunlit half faces Earth; the eight phases repeat about every 29.5 days and are not caused by Earth's shadow.

kid: Something you notice and write down, like a photo of an animal with when and where.
more: A recorded sighting or measurement; on iNaturalist it needs a date, a location and a photo or sound as evidence.
src: iNaturalist Help: How observations become Research Grade

kid: A very long, very deep valley in the ocean floor.
more: A long, narrow, deep trough in the seafloor, often 8 to 10 km deep, formed where one plate sinks beneath another.

kid: The path something takes as it goes around and around another thing in space.
more: A regular, repeating path of one object around another, where forward speed and gravity's pull balance, like the space station around Earth.
src: NASA Space Place: What Is an Orbit?

kid: A way to count tiny amounts: how many bits out of one million.
more: A unit for small amounts; 400 ppm of carbon dioxide means 400 CO2 molecules in every million molecules of dry air.
src: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory: CO2 trends

kid: One of the giant pieces of Earth's hard outer shell, like a cracked eggshell.
more: A huge slab of Earth's rigid outer layer that moves a few centimetres a year; most earthquakes and volcanoes happen where plates meet.

kid: Something made at the time, like a diary, letter or photo.
more: An original item created during the time studied; a secondary source is one made later that explains or interprets the past.
src: Library of Congress: Getting started with primary sources

kid: A long list of careful measurements kept over many years.
more: A long series of measurements of the same thing; NOAA's global temperature record starts in 1850. A 'record high' is the top value in it.

kid: A giant ring around the Pacific Ocean with many volcanoes and earthquakes.
more: The belt of plate boundaries around the Pacific, where the Pacific Plate meets many others; it is the world's most active zone for earthquakes and volcanoes.
src: USGS: What is the Ring of Fire?

kid: Anything that travels around a planet, moon or star, like the Moon or a space station.
more: Any object that orbits a planet, star or moon; natural ones include the Moon, and human-made ones include weather satellites.
src: NASA Space Place: What Is a Satellite?

kid: Frozen ocean water that floats on the sea.
more: Ice that forms, grows and melts in the ocean itself; Arctic sea ice is usually largest in March and smallest in September.
src: NSIDC: Quick facts about sea ice

kid: How high the ocean's surface reaches along the land.
more: The average height of the ocean surface at a place; it rises when land ice like glaciers and ice sheets melts into the ocean.

kid: Where a fact or picture comes from. Always ask who made it and why.
more: The origin of information; check who made it, when, why and for whom, and whether it agrees with other independent sources.
src: Library of Congress: Getting started with primary sources

kid: A group of living things of the same kind that can have babies together.
more: A group of similar organisms that can reproduce with each other; iNaturalist checks that people agree on an observation's species.

kid: When one of Earth's giant plates slides down under another one.
more: At a convergent boundary, one plate sinks beneath another into the mantle, forming trenches, deep earthquakes and volcanoes like the Andes.

kid: The loud boom that lightning makes.
more: The sound of air expanding explosively after lightning heats it; light arrives first, so counting seconds to the boom estimates distance.
src: NOAA SciJinks: What causes lightning and thunder?

kid: What the sky is doing today: sunny, rainy, windy or snowy.
more: Conditions over a short time, from hours to days, like a rainstorm or a hot afternoon; climate is the long-term average.
